title: Weighted Average Calculator (Step by Step)
description: Calculate a weighted average from values and weights given as percentages or plain numbers, with each row's contribution and the working shown.
quickAnswer: A weighted average multiplies each value by its weight, adds the products, and divides by the total weight. Scores of 90 (30%), 80 (50%) and 70 (20%) give 27 + 40 + 14 = 81. With plain-number weights the method is the same: 90 with weight 2 and 80 with weight 3 give (180 + 240) ÷ 5 = 84.

formula.title: Weighted Average Formula
formula.explanation: Each value counts in proportion to its weight. When the weights are percentages that add up to 100, dividing by the total weight is the same as dividing by 100, so each row's contribution is simply value × weight%. If percentage weights add up to something other than 100, the calculator divides by their actual total instead (normalises them) and tells you, which is the same as scaling every weight so that they add up to 100.

commonMistakes.title: Taking a simple average instead
commonMistakes.description: The plain average of 90, 80 and 70 is 80, but if the 90 counts for 30% and the 70 for only 20%, the weighted average is 81. Use the plain average only when every item counts equally.

commonMistakes.title: Dividing by the number of items
commonMistakes.description: A weighted average divides by the total weight, not by how many values there are. Dividing 420 by 2 items instead of 5 weight units gives 210, which is meaningless.

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting missing weight
commonMistakes.description: If assessments worth 20% have not happened yet, your weights add up to 80%. The normalised result shows your average so far; it is not your final grade until the remaining 20% is added.

commonMistakes.title: Mixing weight types
commonMistakes.description: Use one kind of weight for every row: all percentages, or all credit hours, or all quantities. Mixing a 30% weight with a 3-credit weight gives a wrong answer.

commonMistakes.title: Using weights on different scales of values
commonMistakes.description: Make sure every value is on the same scale, for example all percentages. A score of 18/20 should be entered as 90, not 18, if the others are out of 100.

faqs.q: How do you calculate a weighted average?
faqs.a: Multiply each value by its weight, add all the products, then divide by the sum of the weights. For 90 (30%), 80 (50%) and 70 (20%): (2,700 + 4,000 + 1,400) ÷ 100 = 81.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a weighted average and a normal average?
faqs.a: A normal (arithmetic) average gives every value the same importance. A weighted average lets some values count more than others according to their weights.

faqs.q: Do weights have to add up to 100?
faqs.a: No. Any positive weights work because the formula divides by their total. If you choose percentage weights that do not add up to 100, the calculator normalises them and tells you.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my grade with weighted categories?
faqs.a: Enter each category's average as a value and its percentage of the course as the weight. The result is your overall grade; the contribution column shows how many points each category adds.

faqs.q: How do I calculate a weighted average in Excel?
faqs.a: Use =SUMPRODUCT(values, weights)/SUM(weights). For values in A2:A4 and weights in B2:B4: =SUMPRODUCT(A2:A4,B2:B4)/SUM(B2:B4).
Yes. A row with weight 0 has no effect on the result. If every weight is zero there is nothing to average, so the calculator shows an error.

faqs.q: What is a weighted average used for?
faqs.a: Course grades, GPA by credit hours, average purchase price across orders of different sizes, portfolio returns, survey results and index numbers all use weighted averages.

simple-vs-weighted-average.heading: Simple vs Weighted Average
simple-vs-weighted-average.p1: A simple average treats every number the same. A weighted average lets each number count according to how important it is, which is how most course grades, GPAs and price averages are worked out.
simple-vs-weighted-average.caption1: Simple and weighted averages of the same scores
simple-vs-weighted-average.p2: The weighted result is higher because the strongest score (90) carries more weight than the weakest (70).

where-weighted-averages-are-used.heading: Where Weighted Averages Are Used
where-weighted-averages-are-used.li1: Grades: coursework, midterm and final exam weights from a syllabus. For grades by letter, the grade calculator and GPA calculator do this with credit hours.
where-weighted-averages-are-used.li2: Average cost: if you buy 10 units at 5 and 30 units at 6, the average price is (50 + 180) ÷ 40 = 5.75, not 5.50.
where-weighted-averages-are-used.li3: Admissions: merit and aggregate formulas weight school results and entry tests; the merit calculator handles marks out of different totals.
where-weighted-averages-are-used.li4: Statistics: price indexes such as the Consumer Price Index weight each category by its share of household spending.
where-weighted-averages-are-used.p1: All calculations run in your browser. You can share a link that reopens your exact rows.
